Truth is not created by personal conviction.

Human reason can discover and articulate truth, but finite human minds do not thereby become the ultimate source of truth.

The investigation therefore requires an ultimate ground adequate to the objectivity, stability, and reality of truth.

At this point the question of God is no longer an arbitrary insertion into the argument.

It is the question generated by the argument:

> **What ultimately grounds truth and reality?**

The biblical record presents God as far more than a theoretical explanation.

It presents Him as Creator, source, revealer, faithful, unchanging, and inseparably related to truth.

But those claims must be established.

The next movement therefore begins where the present chapter has brought us:

> **God as the Ground of Truth.**

---

# Chapter Reference Notes

## Governing distinctions

| Question | What it asks |
|---|---|
| **What is truth?** | Whether a proposition corresponds to what is actually the case |
| **What is reality?** | What actually exists or obtains |
| **What is belief?** | A person's acceptance of a proposition |
| **What is authority?** | What has standing to govern judgment |
| **What is the ground of truth?** | What ultimately accounts for objective truth |
| **What is revelation?** | Truth communicated from its divine source |
| **What is authentication?** | What warrants recognition of a claimed revelation as genuine |

## Logical guardrails for the next chapters

- Do not infer all divine attributes from the bare proposition that God exists.
- Do not confuse the existence of God with the authentication of Scripture.
- Do not use theological vocabulary as a substitute for biblical demonstration.
- Do not make a philosophical argument carry a conclusion larger than its premises warrant.
- Do not treat every biblical quotation as performing the same evidential function.
- Do not reduce God to a “subject” or topic of human discussion.
- Do not substitute commentary about God for the biblical record concerning God.
- Do not prematurely use Scripture as an already-established infallible authority to prove the premises whose establishment will later ground Scripture's authority.
- Do not abandon reason in order to affirm revelation.
- Do not make reason the creator of the reality it investigates.

## Forward dependency

> **Chapter 8 — Ultimate Authority**  
> ↓  
> **Chapter 9 — What Grounds Truth?**  
> ↓  
> **Chapter 10 — God as the Ground of Truth**  
> ↓  
> **Chapter 11 — Truthfulness, Faithfulness, and Immutability**  
> ↓  
> **Chapter 12 — God Cannot Lie**  
> ↓  
> **Chapter 13 — Knowing God: Revelation Rather Than Speculation**

The argument remains cumulative:

> **Truth → Reality → Knowledge → Evidence → Reason → Authority → Ground → God → Revelation → Scripture → Graphē**

chapters.title: God as the Ground of Truth
chapters.body:
> **Central question:** If truth requires an ultimate ground, in what sense is God that ground?

Chapter 9 brought the investigation to the question of ultimate grounding.

That question cannot be answered merely by attaching the word **God** to the conclusion.

If one says:

> **“God is the ground of truth,”**

the statement contains several distinct propositions that must be examined:

1. that God exists;
2. that God is ultimate rather than one contingent reality among others;
3. that God is the Creator and source of contingent reality;
4. that God is rationally adequate as the ground of reality's intelligibility;
5. that truth is not external to God as though God merely possesses it;
6. that God's nature is intrinsically truthful;
7. that God's Word is therefore trustworthy;
8. and, eventually, that the Bible can be authenticated as a written revelation proceeding from that God.

The present chapter concentrates on the first major transition:

> **from the problem of an ultimate ground to the biblical conception of God as the ultimate ground of truth and reality.**

It is important not to confuse this with the later question of biblical authentication.

The argument must remain ordered.

> **God's existence and nature → divine truthfulness → revelation → authentication of the written record.**

The Bible will eventually become the principal written authority under investigation. But at this stage, the argument must not simply use the Bible as an unexamined premise to establish the very authority for which the Bible will later be examined.

At the same time, neither should the biblical record be treated as though it were merely one opinion among competing religious texts.

The investigation must distinguish **the existence of a claim**, **the evidence for the claim**, and **the authority of the source once authenticated**.

---

# 1. What Would It Mean for God to Be the Ground of Truth?

To call God the ground of truth is stronger than saying:

> “God knows what is true.”

It is also stronger than saying:

> “God usually tells the truth.”

The first describes knowledge.

The second describes reliable communication.

Neither by itself explains the ultimate status of truth.

The stronger proposition is that objective truth is grounded in the reality and nature of God.

That means truth is not an arbitrary rule imposed by God from outside Himself.

Nor is God subject to a higher truth existing independently above Him.

Both alternatives create difficulties.

If truth exists independently of God as a standard above Him, then God is not ultimate with respect to truth.

If God can make contradictory propositions true simply by declaring them true, then truth becomes arbitrary.

The biblical conception points in another direction:

> **God is true.**

This is not merely a statement that God possesses correct information.

It concerns His nature.

---

# 2. God Is Not Being Introduced as a Mere Hypothesis

The word **God** can be used in many different ways.

A philosopher may use it to designate a necessary being.

A theologian may use it within a doctrinal system.

A commentator may describe divine attributes.

A culture may use the word according to inherited tradition.

None of these uses, by themselves, establishes what God actually is.

The present investigation therefore has to distinguish:

> **God Himself**

from

> **human descriptions of God.**

This distinction is particularly important because the question is not:

> “What have theologians said about God?”

The question is:

> **What is the reality to which the term God refers, and what grounds warrant the claims being made about Him?**

That is why the investigation must not be controlled by theological vocabulary alone.

Words such as *omnipotent*, *omniscient*, *immutable*, *transcendent*, *personal*, and *necessary* can be useful.

But definitions are not demonstrations.

A proposition concerning God must still be established.

---

# 3. From Contingent Reality to an Ultimate Ground

The previous chapter distinguished contingent reality from what is necessary.

A contingent reality is one that does not contain within itself a sufficient explanation of why it exists rather than not existing.

The ordinary world presents us with contingent realities everywhere.

Things come into existence.

Things cease to exist.

Things depend upon conditions outside themselves.

A tree depends upon prior causes and sustaining conditions.

A human being depends upon parents, biological processes, environmental conditions, and countless other realities.

Planets, stars, organisms, institutions, and civilizations likewise exhibit dependence.

If every explanation terminates only in another contingent reality, the question remains:

> **Why does the entire dependent order exist at all?**

An ultimate explanation cannot simply be another member of the same dependent order.

If it were, the explanatory question would remain.

This is the force of the classical move toward a necessary ground.

It is not yet a complete demonstration of every divine attribute.

It is a demand for an adequate ultimate explanation.

---

# 4. Why “Necessary” Matters

A necessary reality is not merely a thing that happens to exist for a very long time.

It is a reality whose nonexistence is not a genuine alternative in the relevant sense.

This distinction matters because infinite duration does not by itself equal necessity.

Something could conceivably exist eternally while still requiring an explanation for why it exists.

The issue is not merely:

> **How long has it existed?**

The issue is:

> **Why does it exist at all?**

An ultimate ground must therefore possess a mode of existence adequate to terminate the explanatory dependence of contingent reality.

This is why the argument cannot stop with:

> “The universe exists.”

The existence of the universe is precisely what requires examination.

---

# 5. The Biblical Record Does Not Present God as a Dependent Being

The biblical conception of God is radically different from the conception of God as merely one powerful entity inside the universe.

The opening declaration of Scripture is:

> **“In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.”**  
> — Genesis 1:1

The claim is not that God is one object among the objects He created.

God is presented as the Creator.

The distinction is fundamental:

> **Creator and creation are not equivalent categories.**

If God created all things, then God cannot be merely one contingent component of the created order.

John's Gospel develops this claim concerning the Word:

> **“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”**  
> — John 1:1

And:

> **“All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.”**  
> — John 1:3

The argument is striking.

Everything that was made belongs to the category of things made.

The Word is presented as the agent through whom all things were made.

Therefore the biblical presentation does not place God or the Word within the class of created things.

This is not merely a statement about God's power.

It concerns the very structure of reality.

---

# 6. Why Creation Matters to the Truth Question

The connection between creation and truth is easy to miss.

If God is the Creator of all contingent reality, then reality itself is not an unexplained collection of independent facts.

It has an ultimate source.

And if reality proceeds from an intelligent Creator, the intelligibility of reality is no longer inexplicable in the same way.

The world can be investigated rationally because it is not being treated as the ultimate source of its own intelligibility.

This does not mean every human explanation is correct.

It means that the rational structure of reality is compatible with its being grounded in an intelligent source.

The biblical statement:

> **“In the beginning God created...”**

therefore has implications far beyond cosmology.

It establishes a relationship between:

> **God → creation → reality → intelligibility → knowledge.**

This relationship becomes important when we later ask how finite human beings can know truth about the world and, more importantly, how they can know what God has revealed.

---

# 7. The Word and the Nature of Reality

John 1:1–3 deserves particular attention because of the connection between **the Word** and **creation**.

The text does not present the Word as merely a collection of written sentences.

The Word is presented personally and eternally in relation to God, and John declares:

> **“the Word was God.”**

Then:

> **“All things were made by him.”**

This gives the investigation a profound conceptual connection.

The One through whom all things were made is not detached from truth as though truth were an arbitrary human category imposed upon an otherwise unintelligible universe.

The biblical conception connects divine reality, divine Word, and created reality.

That does not yet establish every doctrine concerning Scripture.

It does, however, establish why the relationship between **God, Word, and truth** cannot be treated superficially.

---

# 8. “I Am the Truth”

The connection becomes even more explicit in the words of Jesus Christ:

> **“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”**  
> — John 14:6

Notice the form of the declaration.

Christ does not merely say:

> “I know the truth.”

Nor:

> “I teach some truths.”

He says:

> **“I am ... the truth.”**

This is a claim about identity, not merely information.

If Christ is truth, then truth is not presented merely as an abstract proposition existing independently of divine reality.

The claim points toward truth as inseparable from the nature and identity of God revealed in Christ.

That is why Christology cannot be postponed indefinitely.

The investigation of the ground of truth eventually encounters the person of Christ.

---

# 9. Is God Merely a Being Who Tells the Truth?

No—that formulation is inadequate to the biblical conception.

A human being can tell the truth while still being capable of falsehood.

A human witness may accurately report one event and misunderstand another.

Human truthfulness is therefore contingent and fallible.

The biblical presentation of God is different.

The relevant question is not:

> “Has God ever happened to tell the truth?”

It is:

> **Is falsehood compatible with God's nature?**

Hebrews 6:17–18 is therefore central:

> **“Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath:  
> That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation...”**

The phrase **“it was impossible for God to lie”** is not merely a statement that God has a good record.

It places falsehood in opposition to God's nature.

That proposition will be developed more fully in Chapter 12.

For the present chapter, its importance is this:

> **If God is the ultimate ground of reality and falsehood is impossible to Him, then truthfulness is not an accidental feature of divine communication.**

It belongs to the identity of the One from whom revelation would proceed.

---

# 10. God as the Unchanging Source

James 1:17 adds another dimension:

> **“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.”**

The text presents God as without the variability associated with changing human conditions.

This matters because an ultimate ground must not itself be merely unstable.

If truth were grounded in a being whose nature continually changed, the investigation would again face the question of what ultimately explains the standard.

The biblical description instead presents God as constant.

That constancy is not merely emotional reliability.

It concerns the character of the One from whom reality and communication proceed.

---

# 11. “Thou Art True”

The biblical record also contains direct recognition of God's truthfulness.

In Mark 12:14, those addressing Jesus say:

> **“Master, we know that thou art true, and carest for no man...”**

The statement is significant because **true** is being attributed to Christ.

It is not merely saying that He knows facts.

It concerns His character and reliability.

This aligns with John 14:6:

> **“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”**

The cumulative picture therefore becomes stronger:

> **God is true.**

> **Christ identifies Himself with truth.**

> **The Word is God.**

> **The Word is the agent of creation.**

> **God does not change.**

> **It is impossible for God to lie.**

These propositions must eventually be brought together carefully.

---

# 12. Truth Is Not Something God Must Discover

There is a crucial philosophical consequence.

If God is the ultimate ground of reality, God does not stand outside reality as a finite investigator attempting to discover whether His own existence corresponds to something else.

Nor does God require a higher authority to tell Him what is true.

If a higher standard existed above God and determined whether God were true, that higher standard would occupy a more ultimate position with respect to truth.

The biblical conception therefore directs the argument toward:

> **truth grounded in God Himself.**

This does not mean that God arbitrarily creates logical contradictions and then calls them true.

Rather, the biblical conception presents God as true and faithful in His own being.

Truth is therefore not an external measuring stick by which God is reluctantly judged.

---

# 13. Is This Circular Reasoning?

A serious objection must be addressed.

Someone may say:

> “You are using the Bible to establish that God is truthful, and then you will use God's truthfulness to establish the Bible.”

If that were the whole argument, it would indeed be circular.

But that is not the intended structure.

The investigation distinguishes two levels.

### Level One — Ground

What rational and evidential considerations establish concerning God, reality, causation, necessity, intelligibility, and divine attributes.

### Level Two — Revelation

Once the existence and nature of God have been sufficiently established, what evidence establishes that a particular claimed revelation actually proceeds from that God?

### Level Three — Written record

Once revelation is established as genuinely divine, what establishes that the particular writings under examination accurately preserve and communicate that revelation?

### Level Four — Authority and interpretation

Once the written record has been authenticated, what does its authority require of the reader, and how should it be interpreted?

This ordering prevents the argument from simply assuming the conclusion.

---

# 14. Does Reason Replace Revelation?

No.

This distinction is essential.

Reason can investigate whether a proposition is coherent.

Reason can compare evidence.

Reason can evaluate testimony.

Reason can infer causes from effects.

Reason can distinguish necessary from contingent explanations.

Reason can test whether a conclusion follows from premises.

But reason cannot manufacture a historical event it did not witness.

Nor can reason simply deduce every particular fact God may choose to reveal.

For example, human reason can ask whether it is possible for God to communicate.

It cannot, merely by abstract reasoning, determine everything God has actually communicated at a particular historical moment.

That requires revelation and evidence concerning the revelation.

Thus:

> **Reason is not the replacement for revelation.**

Rather:

> **Reason is necessary for evaluating the claim that revelation has occurred and for understanding what that revelation communicates.**

This is precisely why the book refuses the false choice between reason and Scripture.

---

# 15. Natural Knowledge and Revealed Knowledge Must Be Distinguished

This distinction also helps prevent confusion concerning the existence of God.

Human beings encounter the created world.

They observe order.

They encounter causation.

They experience moral obligation.

They reason about existence.

They encounter consciousness, rationality, contingency, and intelligibility.

Such considerations can generate arguments concerning God's existence and attributes.

But these arguments are not identical with revelation.

A person may reason from creation toward a Creator.

That does not mean the person has thereby learned every revealed truth concerning God's purposes, covenant, redemption, Christ, or Scripture.

Conversely, revelation does not make rational evaluation irrelevant.

The two domains are related:

> **Reason can investigate reality and assess revelation.**

> **Revelation can disclose realities that human investigation could not independently discover.**

This distinction will become indispensable when the book examines how the Bible was given.

---

# 16. What About the Classical Arguments for God?

The classical arguments remain relevant, but they must be properly classified.

The cosmological argument asks about the ultimate cause or explanation of contingent reality.

The teleological argument examines order, purposiveness, and apparent design.

The moral argument examines objective moral obligation, moral consciousness, and moral order.

These arguments can contribute to a cumulative case.

But none should be made to carry conclusions beyond what its premises establish.

For example:

> **An argument from contingency is not, by itself, a complete demonstration of biblical inspiration.**

Nor is:

> **An argument from design, by itself, a demonstration of the biblical canon.**

The proper role of such reasoning is to investigate the existence and attributes of an ultimate reality.

The question of revelation comes afterward.

This is precisely why the book can engage philosophical arguments without becoming a philosophical apologetics manual.

---

# 17. Why the Biblical Account Still Matters Decisively

There is, however, another danger.

Once philosophical reasoning is introduced, one may begin treating philosophy as though it were a higher authority than the biblical record.

That would reverse the intended architecture.

Philosophical arguments can investigate propositions concerning God.

They cannot replace what God has revealed.

If God has actually spoken, the content of that revelation is not to be reconstructed from human speculation as though revelation were unnecessary.

The crucial distinction is:

> **Arguments can lead us toward conclusions concerning God's existence and attributes; revelation tells us what God has actually revealed.**

Therefore the philosophical investigation is preparatory.

The biblical record becomes decisive once the question changes from:

> **“What can human reason establish concerning God?”**

to:

> **“What has God actually revealed?”**

---

# 18. Why God Is the Proper Candidate for the Ultimate Ground

The cumulative argument can now be stated.

An adequate ultimate ground of truth and reality must be:

- not merely contingent;
- sufficient to account for contingent existence;
- capable of grounding intelligibility;
- adequate to the rational order encountered in reality;
- not dependent upon a higher human authority;
- and, if it is to ground trustworthy revelation, intrinsically truthful.

The biblical conception of God answers these requirements by presenting God as:

> **Creator**

> **ultimate**

> **unchanging**

> **true**

> **faithful**

> **incapable of falsehood**

and as the One through whom all things were made.

The argument is therefore not:

> “The Bible says God is the ground of truth; therefore God is the ground of truth.”

It is:

> **The problem of objective truth and contingent reality requires an adequate ultimate ground; the conception of God presented in the biblical record identifies such a ground; the philosophical and evidential case for God's existence and attributes must then be examined alongside the biblical record; and, once the divine nature is established, the question of divine revelation can be investigated without circularity.**

That is the architecture of the argument.

---

# 19. The Difference Between Grounding Truth and Knowing Truth

Another distinction must remain explicit.

Suppose God is objectively the ground of truth.

That does not mean every human being automatically knows every truth.

The **ground of truth** and the **means of knowing truth** are different questions.

God may ground reality.

Human beings still require appropriate means of knowledge.

Those means include:

- perception;
- memory;
- testimony;
- rational inference;
- historical investigation;
- and, where God communicates what could not otherwise be known, revelation.

Therefore:

> **God's role as the ground of truth is ontological.**

> **Human investigation of truth is epistemological.**

> **Evidence concerns the warrant by which the investigator recognizes truth.**

> **Interpretation concerns the correct understanding of an authoritative communication.**

These distinctions preserve the four-question architecture established at the beginning of the book.

---

# 20. What Does This Do to the Question of the Bible?

It changes the question profoundly.

The investigation is no longer asking:

> “Which religious book do people prefer?”

Nor:

> “Which tradition has the most followers?”

Nor:

> “Which theologian gives the most persuasive explanation?”

The question becomes:

> **Has the God who is the ground of truth actually revealed Himself and communicated truth to humanity?**

If the answer is yes, then the next question is:

> **How was that revelation given?**

And then:

> **How do we know that the writings called the Bible genuinely preserve and communicate that revelation?**

This is where the distinction between **God**, **revelation**, **inspiration**, **written record**, and **canon** becomes essential.

They must not be collapsed into one word.

---

# 21. A Necessary Correction to the Language of “God as Subject”

The phrase “God is the subject of the Bible” is inadequate if it is intended to mean merely that God is a topic discussed by human writers.

The biblical record presents something much stronger.

God is presented as:

- Creator;
- speaker;
- revealer;
- actor in history;
- giver of commandments;
- sender of prophets;
- Father;
- judge;
- and, in the New Testament, revealed in Christ.

Thus God is not merely **the subject about whom the book speaks**.

He is presented as **the living reality who acts, speaks, reveals, and stands behind the communication being recorded**.

That distinction becomes decisive in the next movements.

The question will no longer be merely:

> “What does the Bible say about God?”

It will become:

> **“How did God communicate what He intended humanity to know, and what makes the resulting record trustworthy?”**

---

# 22. What This Chapter Has Established

The chapter has established the conceptual necessity of distinguishing several propositions.

### First

Objective truth cannot simply be grounded in human preference, convention, institutional declaration, or finite cognition.

### Second

Contingent reality requires an adequate ultimate explanation.

### Third

The biblical conception of God presents Him not as a contingent object within creation but as Creator.

### Fourth

John 1:1–3 connects God, the Word, and creation in a manner directly relevant to the relationship between reality and divine Word.

### Fifth

Jesus Christ's declaration:

> **“I am ... the truth”**

makes truth a matter of divine identity rather than merely divine information.

### Sixth

The biblical record presents God as true, faithful, unchanging, and incapable of falsehood.

### Seventh

Those divine attributes are directly relevant to the possibility of trustworthy revelation.

### Eighth

God's existence and nature must not be confused with the later authentication of Scripture.

### Ninth

Reason does not replace revelation; it is required to investigate claims concerning revelation and to understand its content.

### Tenth

The investigation must now move from **God as the ground of truth** to **the attributes that make divine communication trustworthy**.

---

# 23. What Has Not Yet Been Established?

Intellectual discipline requires us to mark the boundary.

This chapter has not yet established:

- the complete biblical doctrine of God's attributes;
- the full argument that God cannot lie;
- the historical authentication of the Bible;
- the modes by which revelation was communicated;
- the meaning of inspiration;
- the authenticity of the biblical documents;
- the canon;
- or the authority of *graphē*.

Those questions belong to subsequent chapters.

The conclusion reached here is narrower but foundational:

> **If truth requires an ultimate ground, the biblical conception of God presents the kind of ultimate reality capable of grounding truth, reality, intelligibility, and trustworthy communication; the truthfulness and immutability of that God must now be examined directly.**

---

# 24. The Question That Must Now Be Answered

We have reached the next necessary question.

If God is the ground of truth, and if divine revelation is to be trusted because it proceeds from God, then we must know more than that God exists.

We must know **what kind of God He is**.

Is He truthful?

Is He faithful?

Does He change?

Can He contradict Himself?

Can He deceive?

Can He lie?

Can His counsel fail?

Can His Word prove false?

These are not secondary theological curiosities.

They determine whether divine revelation could possess the epistemic reliability claimed for it.

The next chapter therefore examines:

> **The Truthfulness, Faithfulness, and Immutability of God.**

---

# Chapter Reference Notes

## Principal biblical texts

- **Genesis 1:1** — God as Creator.
- **John 1:1–3** — the Word, God, and creation.
- **John 14:6** — Christ: “I am ... the truth.”
- **Mark 12:14** — “thou art true.”
- **James 1:17** — no variableness or shadow of turning.
- **Hebrews 6:17–18** — immutability and the impossibility of God lying.
- **2 Corinthians 1:18** — God's faithfulness.
- **John 17:17** — “thy word is truth.”

## Conceptual distinctions preserved

| Distinction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **God** | The ultimate divine reality under investigation |
| **Ground of truth** | That upon which objective truth ultimately depends |
| **Truthfulness** | The conformity of God's nature and communication to truth |
| **Revelation** | Divine communication of what is made known |
| **Inspiration** | The divine superintendence involved in the communication and recording of Scripture |
| **Written record** | The documentary form in which revelation/testimony is preserved |
| **Authentication** | The evidential process by which a claimed revelation or document is established as genuine |
| **Authority** | The right or standing to govern judgment |
| **Interpretation** | Correctly understanding what an authoritative communication means |

## Argumentative guardrails

- Do not use Scripture circularly to establish Scripture before its authenticity is examined.
- Do not use philosophy as a replacement for revelation.
- Do not confuse an argument for God's existence with an argument for biblical inspiration.
- Do not infer every divine attribute from one argument.
- Do not treat God as merely a topic invented by biblical writers.
- Do not reduce Christ's claim “I am ... the truth” to “Christ teaches true things.”
- Do not reduce God's truthfulness to a statistical history of accurate statements.
- Do not confuse the ground of truth with the human means by which truth is known.
- Do not allow the existence of human interpretations to obscure the distinction between God and human accounts about God.
- Do not turn cumulative evidence into a collection of disconnected proof texts.

## Forward movement

> **Truth**  
> ↓  
> **Ultimate ground**  
> ↓  
> **God**  
> ↓  
> **Truthfulness / Faithfulness / Immutability**  
> ↓  
> **Impossible for God to lie**  
> ↓  
> **Revelation**  
> ↓  
> **Authentication**  
> ↓  
> **Written Record**  
> ↓  
> **Graphē / Holy Writ**  
> ↓  
> **Authority**  
> ↓  
> **Interpretation**

The investigation therefore remains cumulative.

Each conclusion supplies premises required by the next question.

chapters.title: The Truthfulness, Faithfulness, and Immutability of God
chapters.body:
> **Central question:** If God is the ground of truth, what is it about God's own nature that makes Him a trustworthy ground of truth and revelation?

Chapter 10 established the necessity of moving from the question of an ultimate ground to the nature of that ground.

It also established an important boundary.

It is not enough to say:

> **“God exists.”**

Nor is it enough to say:

> **“God is powerful.”**

If God is to be the ultimate ground of truth, and if a later written revelation is to be regarded as trustworthy because it proceeds from God, then God's relationship to truth must itself be established.

The question is therefore not merely whether God possesses information.

It is not merely whether God has spoken.

It is not even merely whether God has historically made promises.

The deeper question is:

> **What is God like with respect to truth, faithfulness, constancy, and falsehood?**

That question is necessary because the reliability of communication depends upon the reliability of its source.

If a source can deceive, its statements require independent correction.

If a source is capable of error, its testimony cannot simply function as an infallible standard.

But if the source is intrinsically true, faithful, unchanging, and incapable of falsehood, then the epistemological status of what that source communicates is radically different.

This chapter therefore develops the divine attributes that make the next question possible.

Chapter 12 will then take one of them—the impossibility of God lying—and examine it with greater precision.

---

# 1. The Source Must Be Examined Before the Communication

Suppose a person receives a document claiming:

> “God said this.”

The statement contains two distinct claims.

First:

> **God exists and is capable of communicating.**

Second:

> **This particular communication genuinely came from God.**

But even before those questions can be resolved, another issue arises:

> **What kind of source is God?**

If the alleged source were known to be deceptive, the claim would require immediate suspicion.

If the source were known to be unreliable, the claim could not be accepted merely because it was attributed to that source.

If the source were perfectly truthful and incapable of falsehood, however, a genuine communication from that source would carry a very different epistemic status.

Therefore:

> **The character of the source is relevant to the credibility of the communication.**

This does not mean that every document claiming divine origin is automatically genuine.

That would collapse **divine truthfulness** into **documentary authentication**, which the book has deliberately refused to do.

The correct order is:

> **God's truthfulness → possibility of trustworthy revelation → evidence for a claimed revelation → authentication of the written record.**

Each step still has to be established.

---

# 2. Truthfulness Is More Than Accurate Speech

A person can accidentally speak something true.

A person can also communicate a correct statement while misunderstanding the subject.

Truthfulness, however, concerns more than the accidental correspondence of an isolated sentence with reality.

It concerns the character of the communicator.

A truthful person does not intentionally present falsehood as truth.

When the Bible describes God as true, therefore, the claim concerns God's character and reliability.

This distinction matters because the book is not trying to establish merely:

> “God has said some true things.”

It is asking whether:

> **truth belongs intrinsically to God.**

That is a much stronger proposition.

If truthfulness were merely occasional in God, then the human investigator would still require an independent standard for deciding when God's statements could be trusted.

But if God is true in His very nature, the situation changes.

---

# 3. “God Is True”

The biblical record repeatedly attributes truthfulness to God.

The declaration in Mark 12:14 is especially direct:

> **“Master, we know that thou art true, and carest for no man...”**

The statement is addressed to Jesus Christ.

It does not merely praise Him as someone who occasionally teaches correct propositions.

It identifies Him as **true**.

This must be read alongside His own declaration in John 14:6:

> **“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”**

The significance is substantial.

Christ does not merely claim to possess truth as information.

He identifies Himself with **the truth**.

That moves the discussion from:

> “What does God know?”

to:

> **“What is God in relation to truth?”**

This is one reason Christ cannot be treated merely as an evidential footnote later in the book.

The investigation of divine truthfulness ultimately encounters Christ's own identity claims.

---

# 4. Truthfulness and the Nature of God

If God is true, then falsehood cannot be treated as a normal alternative available to God in the way that it is available to human beings.

Human beings can know something to be true and nevertheless lie about it.

They can misunderstand.

They can deceive.

They can change their statements.

They can make promises they later abandon.

They can sincerely report what is false because they are mistaken.

None of these limitations can simply be transferred to God.

The biblical record establishes a fundamentally different picture.

Numbers 23:19 states:

> **“God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?”**

The argument is not:

> “God has a very good record of honesty.”

The contrast is deeper:

> **“God is not a man, that he should lie.”**

The text connects God's inability to lie with the distinction between God and man.

This does not mean that God lacks the capacity to communicate or act freely.

It means that falsehood is incompatible with who He is.

That distinction becomes decisive when Hebrews 6:17–18 is examined directly in Chapter 12.

---

# 5. Faithfulness: When God Speaks, His Word Corresponds to His Character

Truthfulness concerns what God is.

Faithfulness concerns the reliability with which God acts according to what He has said.

The two belong together.

A being could theoretically tell the truth about the present while failing to keep promises concerning the future.

Biblical faithfulness goes beyond accurate description.

It includes dependable correspondence between God's Word and God's action.

Deuteronomy 7:9 declares:

> **“Know therefore that the LORD thy God, he is God, the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations.”**

The text does not merely say that God makes covenants.

It identifies Him as **the faithful God** and connects that faithfulness with keeping covenant.

This is important for revelation because revelation is not merely a set of abstract propositions.

The biblical record repeatedly presents God speaking, promising, commanding, warning, acting, and fulfilling.

Faithfulness therefore links:

> **God's character → God's Word → God's action.**

That connection is essential to the reliability of divine communication.

---

# 6. God's Faithfulness Is Not Created by Human Verification

A necessary distinction must be made here.

When human beings investigate whether God is faithful, they are not creating God's faithfulness by their investigation.

They are discovering, testing, or reasoning about a property that is claimed to belong to God.

This is the same distinction used throughout the book:

> **Evidence does not create reality.**

Evidence provides grounds for recognizing reality.

If God is faithful, He is faithful whether a human being recognizes it or not.

If God is true, He is true whether a human institution accepts the proposition or not.

The epistemological task is therefore:

> **How do we rationally establish what is already the case?**

That distinction prevents a common error.

Human consensus does not manufacture divine truthfulness.

The task is to determine whether the evidence and biblical record warrant the conclusion.

---

# 7. Immutability: Why Constancy Matters

Truthfulness and faithfulness would be significantly weakened if God's nature were unstable.

If God were constantly changing in the relevant sense, then the investigator could ask:

> “Which God are we talking about?”

Or:

> “Was what God revealed yesterday still true today?”

The biblical record does not present God in this way.

James 1:17 states:

> **“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.”**

The statement concerns the absence of variability and changing shadow in God.

The significance for the present investigation is not that God never acts differently in different circumstances.

Rather, His character is not subject to the instability that characterizes finite creatures.

His goodness is not temporary.

His truthfulness is not seasonal.

His faithfulness is not dependent upon changing human opinion.

His character does not become true or false according to circumstances.

---

# 8. Immutability Does Not Mean Inactivity

A common misunderstanding must be prevented.

To say that God is immutable does not mean that God cannot act.

The biblical record is filled with divine action.

God creates.

God speaks.

God judges.

God promises.

God delivers.

God sends.

God reveals.

God responds to human actions in history.

Immutability concerns God's **nature and character**, not the proposition that God never acts or that every divine action occurs in exactly the same manner.

This distinction is necessary because otherwise “unchanging” could be misunderstood as philosophical staticness.

The biblical concern is deeper:

> **The God who acts in history does not become a different kind of God while doing so.**

The God who promises remains faithful to His promise.

The God who speaks truth does not become false.

The God who establishes His counsel does not abandon it because His character has changed.

---

# 9. God's Counsel and the Stability of His Purpose

Hebrews 6:17–18 provides an especially important connection between God's purpose, His oath, His immutability, and His inability to lie:

> **“Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath:  
> That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation...”**

The text places several ideas together:

1. God has counsel.
2. God's counsel is immutable.
3. God confirms His promise.
4. The things involved are immutable.
5. It is impossible for God to lie.

The order matters.

The writer is not presenting God's truthfulness as an isolated philosophical attribute.

The impossibility of falsehood is embedded in God's unchanging purpose and His trustworthy promise.

This is why Chapter 12 will need to examine the passage closely rather than merely quoting the phrase:

> **“it was impossible for God to lie.”**

The question is:

> **Why is lying impossible for God?**

The answer must be grounded in what God is, not merely in what God happens to do.

---

# 10. God's Word and God's Character

A source's communication cannot be separated indefinitely from the source itself.

If God is true, then God's Word cannot be treated as though it were independent of His nature.

This does not yet prove that every document claiming to be God's Word actually is God's Word.

That remains an authentication question.

But it establishes an important conditional principle:

> **If a communication genuinely proceeds from the God who is true and incapable of falsehood, its truthfulness cannot be treated as an accidental possibility.**

The question then becomes:

> **How do we establish that the communication genuinely proceeds from God?**

That is the transition to revelation and authentication.

The present chapter therefore establishes the **source-side premise**.

Later chapters will examine the **communication-side evidence**.

---

# 11. God Does Not Need an External Moral Correction

Another consequence follows.

If God is intrinsically true and faithful, then God's moral character is not being measured by a higher external human standard.

This is important because a common philosophical formulation asks:

> “Is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?”

The question can become misleading if it assumes that God is merely an agent who receives moral standards from somewhere else.

The biblical conception presents God Himself as the ultimate reality under investigation.

The relevant issue is not that God arbitrarily manufactures goodness.

Nor is it that God is judged by a superior moral authority.

Rather:

> **God's character is the standard against which His own acts and communications are understood.**

This is another reason the doctrine of divine truthfulness is ontological before it becomes merely ethical.

---

# 12. Truth, Faithfulness, and Immutability Form a Single Epistemic Structure

These attributes should not be studied as disconnected theological labels.

They answer different aspects of one question.

### Truthfulness asks:

> **Is God true rather than false?**

### Faithfulness asks:

> **Can God's Word and commitments be depended upon?**

### Immutability asks:

> **Does His character and counsel remain stable rather than becoming something else?**

Together they yield:

> **God is true, His Word is dependable, and His character does not change into its opposite.**

That combination is precisely what makes trustworthy revelation possible.

If God were true but unreliable in keeping His Word, revelation would remain unstable.

If God were faithful but capable of becoming false, His future communications could not be secured.

If God were immutable but intrinsically false, His constancy would merely make falsehood permanent.

The three concepts therefore work together.

> **Truthfulness gives the content reliability.**

> **Faithfulness gives God's commitments dependability.**

> **Immutability gives the source stability.**

---

# 13. Why This Matters for Divine Revelation

We can now see why the question of revelation could not properly have been placed before this examination.

Suppose God were merely powerful.

Power does not entail truthfulness.

Suppose God were merely intelligent.

Intelligence does not entail moral fidelity.

Suppose God were merely eternal.

Eternity does not entail truth.

Suppose God were merely the Creator.

Creatorship alone, without consideration of God's character, would not establish the reliability of every alleged communication attributed to Him.

Therefore:

> **The existence of God is not the whole argument for trustworthy revelation.**

The nature of God matters.

This is why the book's architecture moves:

> **God → truthfulness → faithfulness → immutability → inability to lie → revelation.**

The sequence is not decorative.

Each stage supplies what the next requires.

---

# 14. Does This Prove Every Claimed Revelation?

No.

This distinction must be protected rigorously.

From:

> **God is truthful**

we cannot validly infer:

> **Therefore every person who says “God told me” is telling the truth.**

That would be an obvious non sequitur.

Likewise:

> **God cannot lie**

does not entail:

> **Every document claiming divine origin is inspired.**

A human being can falsely attribute a statement to God.

A document can contain a false attribution.

A copy can contain a transmission error.

A commentator can misunderstand a text.

An institution can attach God's name to its own doctrine.

Therefore the authenticity of a claimed revelation remains an evidential question.

The correct inference is narrower:

> **If God genuinely communicates something, the truthfulness of that communication is secured by the truthfulness of God.**

The remaining question is whether the alleged communication genuinely came from Him.

---

# 15. God’s Truthfulness Does Not Eliminate the Need for Evidence

This point is crucial for the epistemology of the book.

Someone might reason:

> “If God cannot lie, then there is no need to examine evidence.”

That does not follow.

The impossibility of God lying concerns the truthfulness of God.

Evidence concerns whether the thing before us actually comes from God.

Consider the difference between these propositions:

**P1:** God cannot lie.

**P2:** This document is God's Word.

**P3:** Therefore every proposition in this document is true.

P1 does not establish P2.

But:

> **P1 + P2 → P3**

can become a legitimate form of reasoning once P2 has itself been established.

That distinction will become one of the central epistemological safeguards of the book.

The source can be perfectly truthful while an alleged document falsely claiming to represent that source is not.

---

# 16. Why This Prevents Circularity

The distinction also prevents the argument from becoming circular.

A circular argument would reason:

> “The Bible is God's Word because the Bible says it is God's Word; therefore everything in the Bible is true because the Bible is God's Word.”

That does not independently establish the premise.

The present architecture is different.

It proceeds:

> **What is truth?**

↓

> **What grounds truth?**

↓

> **What can be established concerning God?**

↓

> **What is God's nature with respect to truth and falsehood?**

↓

> **What would follow if God genuinely revealed something?**

↓

> **What evidence establishes that a particular revelation genuinely came from God?**

↓

> **What evidence establishes that a particular written record preserves that revelation?**

This is cumulative reasoning.

The later conclusion does not simply appear at the beginning as an assumption.

---

# 17. God’s Faithfulness in the Biblical Record Is Historical, Not Merely Abstract

The biblical presentation of God's faithfulness is repeatedly connected with events.

God makes promises.

God enters covenants.

God acts.

God delivers.

God judges.

God fulfills.

This is important because the investigation will eventually require historical evidence.

If the Bible merely offered an abstract definition:

> “God is faithful,”

the claim would still require examination.

But the biblical record repeatedly presents God's faithfulness through actions and fulfilled declarations.

This creates a historical dimension to the argument.

The question eventually becomes:

> **Do the events recorded in the biblical writings correspond to reality, and do the patterns of promise and fulfillment support the claim that God is faithful?**

That question belongs to the cumulative authentication process.

The present chapter supplies the conceptual framework within which such evidence becomes intelligible.

---

# 18. God's Character and the Meaning of Revelation

If revelation is communication from God, then revelation cannot be understood independently of the nature of its source.

The source is:

> **true**

therefore His genuine communication is not false.

The source is:

> **faithful**

therefore His promises and declarations are dependable.

The source is:

> **immutable**

therefore His truthfulness is not subject to a later reversal of character.

The source is:

> **incapable of falsehood**

therefore genuine divine communication cannot contain deliberate divine deception.

These conclusions do not yet settle the question of inspiration.

They establish why inspiration, once established, matters.

---

# 19. The Special Significance of 2 Corinthians 1:18

Paul makes a striking statement:

> **“But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay.”**

The phrase begins with:

> **“As God is true...”**

God's truthfulness is being used as the foundation for the reliability of what is being said.

This is important because it shows the biblical pattern itself:

> **God's character → reliability of communication.**

The argument is not a modern philosophical invention imposed upon Scripture.

The biblical record itself connects the truthfulness of God with the reliability of what proceeds from Him.

That connection is essential to the present investigation.

---

# 20. Christ's Truthfulness Brings the Argument Into Focus

The earlier references to Christ can now be brought together.

John 14:6 records:

> **“I am the way, the truth, and the life...”**

Mark 12:14 records the recognition:

> **“Master, we know that thou art true...”**

John 1:1 states:

> **“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”**

John 1:3 continues:

> **“All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.”**

These passages place Christ within the investigation at a level that cannot be reduced to “a teacher who said true things.”

The Word is presented as God.

The Word is presented as involved in creation.

Christ identifies Himself with truth.

Christ is described as true.

This will become decisive later when the book examines:

- Christ's treatment of Scripture;
- His use of Scripture in argument;
- His confirmation of the written record;
- His authority over the apostles;
- and the apostolic testimony concerning Him.

The investigation is therefore moving toward Christ not as an incidental religious figure, but as a central axis in the authentication of divine revelation.

---

# 21. What Does “Immutable” Actually Protect?

The importance of immutability can be stated precisely.

If God were capable of becoming morally or epistemically opposite to what He is, then a revelation authenticated at one point would require continual re-evaluation based on whether God's nature had changed.

But the biblical conception denies that instability.

James 1:17 speaks of:

> **“no variableness, neither shadow of turning.”**

Hebrews 6:17 speaks of:

> **“the immutability of his counsel.”**

The issue is therefore not that God cannot interact dynamically with history.

The issue is that His essential character and purpose are not subject to corruption, contradiction, or reversal.

That stability is essential for trustworthy revelation.

---

# 22. The Three Attributes Answer Three Different Threats

It is useful to identify the threats these attributes answer.

### Threat 1 — Falsehood

If God could lie, His communication could not be treated as inherently trustworthy.

**Answer:** truthfulness.

### Threat 2 — Unreliability

If God did not keep His Word, knowing that He had spoken truth would not guarantee that His commitments would be fulfilled.

**Answer:** faithfulness.

### Threat 3 — Instability

If God's character or counsel could fundamentally change, what was reliable yesterday might not remain reliable tomorrow.

**Answer:** immutability.

Together:

> **Truthfulness → no falsehood.**

> **Faithfulness → dependable Word and promise.**

> **Immutability → enduring stability of character and counsel.**

This is the epistemic significance of the three attributes.

---

# 23. The Argument Has Not Yet Reached Scripture

This boundary must remain explicit.

At this point, the book has not yet demonstrated:

- that the Bible is the Word of God;
- that every biblical book belongs to the canon;
- that every biblical writer was inspired;
- that every manuscript transmission was error-free;
- that every interpretation of Scripture is correct;
- or that every statement made by every person recorded in Scripture represents divine speech.

Those are different propositions.

The present conclusion is narrower:

> **The biblical conception of God presents Him as true, faithful, and unchanging; these attributes are directly relevant to whether divine communication can be trustworthy.**

The next chapter will focus specifically on the strongest formulation:

> **“It was impossible for God to lie.”**

That proposition must not be diluted into the weaker statement:

> “God normally tells the truth.”

The stronger claim has stronger consequences and requires stronger reasoning.

---

# 24. Why “God Cannot Lie” Is More Than a Moral Statement

If lying were merely something God chose not to do, the proposition would describe behavior.

But Hebrews 6:18 uses stronger language:

> **“it was impossible for God to lie.”**

The distinction is enormous.

“God does not lie” can be heard as:

> God chooses not to lie.

“It is impossible for God to lie” points toward:

> **falsehood is incompatible with God's nature.**

The epistemological consequence is correspondingly stronger.

If falsehood is intrinsically incompatible with God, then genuine divine revelation cannot be treated as though God might deliberately communicate falsehood.

This is why the question of God's inability to lie deserves its own chapter.

---

# 25. What This Chapter Has Established

The argument can now be summarized without reducing it to slogans.

### 1. The character of a source matters to the credibility of its communication.

A source that is deceptive or unreliable cannot simply function as an infallible authority.

### 2. Biblical truthfulness concerns God's nature.

The issue is not merely whether God has occasionally spoken correct propositions.

### 3. God is presented as true.

The biblical record explicitly attributes truth to God and to Christ.

### 4. God is faithful.

His faithfulness is connected with His covenant, promises, and actions.

### 5. God is immutable.

His character and counsel are not subject to the instability that characterizes finite beings.

### 6. These attributes belong together.

Truthfulness, faithfulness, and immutability jointly explain why genuine divine communication can be trusted.

### 7. These attributes do not authenticate every claim made in God's name.

The authenticity of a particular revelation or document remains an evidential question.

### 8. The distinction prevents circular reasoning.

The book can establish God's truthfulness without simply assuming that every later document claiming divine origin is authentic.

### 9. Christ occupies a central place in the argument.

His identity as truth, His relation to the Word, and His historical treatment of Scripture will become increasingly important.

### 10. The next question is unavoidable.

If falsehood is impossible for God, **why is it impossible?**

---

# 26. What Has Not Yet Been Established?

The following remain open questions:

- Why exactly is it impossible for God to lie?
- What does the impossibility of divine falsehood mean philosophically and biblically?
- Does divine omnipotence include the ability to do what contradicts God's nature?
- How do God's truthfulness and logical coherence relate?
- What does Scripture mean when it says God cannot lie?
- How does God's inability to lie affect divine promises?
- How does it affect revelation?
- How does it affect inspiration?
- How does it affect the claim that Scripture is infallible?
- What evidence is required to move from **“God cannot lie”** to **“this written record genuinely comes from God”**?

These questions must not be prematurely answered here.

They generate the next chapter.

---

# 27. The Next Necessary Question

We have established that the biblical conception of God is not merely:

> **a powerful being who happens to communicate truth.**

God is presented as:

> **true;**

> **faithful;**

> **unchanging;**

and therefore as a source whose genuine communication cannot be treated as ordinary fallible human testimony.

But one statement demands closer examination:

> **“It was impossible for God to lie.”**

Why?

Is the statement merely saying that God has chosen never to lie?

Or does it mean that falsehood is metaphysically and morally incompatible with God's nature?

If so:

> **What does that impossibility entail for God's Word, His promises, His revelation, and eventually the written record that claims to preserve His revelation?**

That is the question of the next chapter.

---

# Chapter Reference Notes

## Principal biblical texts

- **Numbers 23:19** — God is not man that He should lie; His Word is dependable.
- **Deuteronomy 7:9** — God as the faithful God who keeps covenant.
- **Mark 12:14** — Christ described as true.
- **John 1:1–3** — the Word, God, and creation.
- **John 14:6** — Christ: “I am ... the truth.”
- **James 1:17** — no variableness or shadow of turning.
- **2 Corinthians 1:18** — “God is true.”
- **Hebrews 6:17–18** — immutability of God's counsel and impossibility of God lying.

## Conceptual distinctions

| Concept | What it establishes |
|---|---|
| **Truthfulness** | Falsehood is incompatible with God's truthful nature |
| **Faithfulness** | God's Word, covenant, and commitments can be depended upon |
| **Immutability** | God's essential character and counsel are not unstable or subject to reversal |
| **Revelation** | What God communicates |
| **Authentication** | What establishes that a claimed communication genuinely proceeds from God |
| **Inspiration** | The divine operation concerning the production of Scripture |
| **Infallibility** | The conclusion concerning the truthfulness/reliability of the inspired record |

## Logical guardrails

- Do not infer that every statement attributed to God is genuine merely because God is truthful.
- Do not confuse God's inability to lie with the inability of human beings to falsely claim divine authority.
- Do not use the truthfulness of God as a shortcut around historical authentication.
- Do not treat faithfulness as merely emotional reliability.
- Do not treat immutability as inactivity or inability to act in history.
- Do not reduce “God is true” to “God has accurate information.”
- Do not collapse revelation, inspiration, canon, transmission, authentication, and infallibility into one concept.
- Do not use theological labels without establishing what the underlying biblical propositions actually mean.
- Do not allow a conclusion to outrun its premises.
- Do not replace the biblical record with commentary about the biblical record.

## Forward movement

> **God as ground of truth**
>
> ↓
>
> **God is true**
>
> ↓
>
> **God is faithful**
>

>

>

>

>
> ↓
>
> **What does this guarantee about divine communication?**
>
> ↓
>
> **How can a claimed revelation be authenticated?**
>
> ↓
>
> **How was revelation given and recorded?**
>
> ↓
>
> **What is the Bible?**
>
> ↓
>
> **What is Graphē / Holy Writ?**

chapters.title: God Cannot Lie
chapters.body:
> **Central question:** Why is it impossible for God to lie, and what does that impossibility establish about the trustworthiness of genuine divine communication?

Chapter 11 established three closely related features of God's nature:

> **God is true.**

> **God is faithful.**

> **God is immutable.**

Those conclusions were necessary, but they did not yet answer the strongest question raised by the biblical record.

The question is not merely:

> **Does God tell the truth?**

Nor merely:

> **Has God proved faithful?**

Nor even:

> **Does God remain consistent?**

The stronger biblical claim is:

> **“It was impossible for God to lie.”**  
> — Hebrews 6:18

That statement requires careful treatment.

If it merely meant that God has made a moral decision never to lie, it would tell us something important about His conduct. But Hebrews does not use merely behavioral language. It speaks of **impossibility**.

The question therefore becomes:

> **Why is lying impossible for God?**

The answer cannot simply be:

> “Because the Bible says God cannot lie.”

That would repeat the proposition without explaining it.

Nor can the answer be:

> “Because God chooses not to lie.”

That reduces impossibility to preference.

The investigation must go deeper:

> **What is God such that falsehood is incompatible with Him?**

That question belongs exactly here in the architecture of the book. The preceding chapters established truth, the ground of truth, and the truthfulness, faithfulness, and immutability of God. This chapter now draws those strands together and examines the impossibility of divine falsehood before the book turns to revelation.

---

# 1. “God Cannot Lie” Is Stronger Than “God Does Not Lie”

The first distinction is linguistic and logical.

There is a significant difference between:

> **God does not lie**

and:

> **God cannot lie.**

A statement that someone does not lie may describe a pattern of conduct.

A statement that someone cannot lie concerns a limitation—or, in this case, an incompatibility—within the nature of the subject.

Hebrews 6:18 says:

> **“it was impossible for God to lie.”**

Titus 1:2 likewise speaks of:

> **“God, that cannot lie.”**

The biblical language therefore does not merely establish an excellent record of divine honesty.

It establishes something more fundamental:

> **Falsehood is incompatible with God.**

That distinction matters enormously for the epistemological argument.

If God merely happened never to lie, then the possibility of divine falsehood would remain conceptually open. A person could ask:

> “What prevents God from saying something false tomorrow?”

But if falsehood is impossible for God because it is incompatible with His nature, then the question changes.

The issue is no longer:

> “Has God chosen to be truthful?”

It becomes:

> **“Can the God who is truth cease to be truthful?”**

The biblical answer is no.

---

# 2. What Would a Lie Actually Require?

To understand the force of the biblical claim, we should first understand what a lie is.

A lie is not simply an inaccurate sentence.

An inaccurate statement may result from:

- ignorance;
- mistaken perception;
- defective memory;
- confusion;
- inadequate information;
- faulty inference;
- or deception.

A lie involves something more specific: the communication of falsehood as though it were true, with the relevant intention of deceiving or misrepresenting reality.

That distinction matters because God is not presented as a finite knower who discovers reality gradually and may then misreport what He has discovered.

The biblical conception presents God as:

- the Creator;
- the source of existence;
- the knower of reality;
- true;
- faithful;
- holy;
- unchanging;
- and incapable of falsehood.

Therefore the question is not:

> “Could God make a factual mistake?”

as though God were a finite observer.

The biblical question is deeper:

> **Could falsehood proceed from the One whose nature is truth?**

The answer is no.

---

# 3. Truth Is Not Something God Merely Consults

This point follows from Chapter 10.

If truth were something external to God—a standard existing above Him to which He must conform—then God would not be the ultimate ground of truth.

He would be another knower standing under a higher standard.

But the investigation has already distinguished:

> **truth as reality and correspondence**

from:

> **human recognition of truth.**

God does not become truthful because human beings verify Him.

Human verification discovers what is true.

Likewise, God does not become truthful because He conforms to an external human standard.

The biblical conception presents God Himself as true.

Christ says:

> **“I am ... the truth.”**  
> — John 14:6

Paul writes:

> **“as God is true...”**  
> — 2 Corinthians 1:18

The biblical record therefore does not merely portray God as a being who possesses correct information.

It presents truth as belonging to His identity.

This is why the statement that God cannot lie has ontological significance.

Falsehood is not merely something God dislikes.

It is incompatible with who He is.

---

# 4. “God Is Not a Man, That He Should Lie”

Numbers 23:19 gives one of the clearest biblical contrasts:

> **“God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent...”**

The verse does more than condemn lying.

It contrasts God with human beings.

Human beings are finite.

They can:

- lack knowledge;
- misperceive reality;
- forget;
- contradict themselves;
- change their minds;
- break promises;
- deceive;
- and deliberately misrepresent what they know.

The verse refuses to transfer these limitations to God.

It then immediately connects God's truthfulness with the reliability of His Word:

> **“hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?”**

Notice the structure.

God:

> **says**

and therefore:

> **does.**

God:

> **speaks**

and therefore:

> **fulfills.**

The passage joins speech, truthfulness, faithfulness, and action.

This is exactly why Chapter 11 established faithfulness before Chapter 12.

The God who speaks is not a source whose statements must be treated as provisional guesses.

His Word corresponds to His nature and His action.

---

# 5. Titus 1:2 — “God, That Cannot Lie”

Titus 1:2 is unusually direct:

> **“In hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began.”**

Three ideas appear together:

1. God;
2. His inability to lie;
3. His promise.

The order is significant.

The promise is trustworthy because the One who makes it **cannot lie**.

The text does not say:

> “God promised, and we hope He keeps His promise.”

The credibility of the promise is grounded in the character of the Promiser.

This gives us an important epistemological principle:

> **The reliability of a communication is inseparable from the reliability of its source.**

But this principle must still be applied carefully.

Titus 1:2 does not mean:

> “Any statement anyone attributes to God must be true.”

It means:

> **What genuinely proceeds from God cannot be false because God cannot lie.**

That distinction will become indispensable when the book later examines the authentication of claimed revelation.

---

# 6. Hebrews 6:17–18 — The Strongest Formulation

Hebrews 6:17–18 brings the argument together:

> **“Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath:  
> That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation...”**

The passage does not present God's inability to lie in isolation.

It places it within a structure involving:

- God's purpose;
- His counsel;
- immutability;
- promise;
- oath;
- and the impossibility of falsehood.

The writer is therefore showing why the recipients can possess strong confidence.

The confidence does not rest upon human optimism.

It rests upon the character of God.

The logic can be represented as:

> **God's counsel is immutable**
>
> ↓
>
> **God confirms His promise**
>
> ↓
>
> **the confirming realities are immutable**
>
> ↓
>
> **it is impossible for God to lie**
>
> ↓
>
> **therefore the promise provides strong ground for confidence.**

The important point is that the writer does not say merely:

> “God probably will not lie.”

The impossibility of lying is presented as a foundation for confidence.

---

# 7. Why Is It Impossible?

We can now answer the central question.

> **Why is it impossible for God to lie?**

Because, in the biblical conception, falsehood is incompatible with God's nature.

God is not merely a powerful person who happens to possess moral preferences.

He is presented as true.

Christ says:

> **“I am ... the truth.”**

The biblical record says:

> **“God is true.”**

And Hebrews says:

> **“it was impossible for God to lie.”**

These statements belong together.

The reasoning is:

1. A lie is falsehood presented deceptively as truth.
2. God is true.
3. God does not merely possess truth; truth is attributed to His very nature.
4. Falsehood is therefore incompatible with that nature.
5. Consequently, God cannot lie.

This is not an argument from God's statistical history of honesty.

It is an argument from His nature.

---

# 8. Does “Cannot” Mean God Lacks Power?

A serious question arises here.

If God is omnipotent, what can it mean to say that He **cannot** do something?

The answer requires a distinction between power and contradiction.

To say:

> **God cannot lie**

does not mean that God encounters an external force stronger than Himself.

It does not mean that some independent authority prevents Him from lying.

It means that lying is incompatible with what God is.

The distinction is similar to the difference between:

> **having power**

and:

> **being able to make a contradiction true.**

The existence of divine power does not turn contradictions into realities.

If a proposition is intrinsically contradictory, omnipotence does not make the contradiction coherent.

Likewise, if falsehood is incompatible with God's nature, His inability to lie is not a weakness.

It is a consequence of His perfection.

God's inability to lie is therefore not evidence against omnipotence.

It is evidence concerning the kind of being God is.

---

# 9. “Cannot Lie” Does Not Mean “Cannot Speak”

Another distinction is equally important.

God's inability to lie does not mean God is incapable of communication.

Quite the opposite.

The biblical record presents God as a speaking God.

He:

- speaks;
- commands;
- reveals;
- promises;
- warns;
- testifies;
- sends;
- teaches;
- and communicates.

The question is not whether God can speak.

The question is whether falsehood can genuinely proceed from Him.

The biblical answer is:

> **No.**

This becomes essential when we later examine the ways the biblical record says God communicated:

- by His audible voice;
- through angels;
- through prophets;
- through Christ;
- through apostles;
- through visions;
- through dreams;
- through revelation;
- and through inspired Scripture.

The impossibility of falsehood establishes the **source-side reliability** of genuine divine communication.

It does not by itself authenticate every alleged communication.

---

# 10. Truthfulness and the Possibility of Divine Revelation

The argument has now reached an important bridge.

If God cannot lie, then genuine divine revelation cannot be false.

That conclusion follows only conditionally:

> **If God genuinely revealed it, then it is true.**

This is different from:

> **If someone says God revealed it, then it is true.**

The first follows from God's nature.

The second does not.

This distinction is indispensable.

Suppose a person writes:

> “God told me X.”

There are now at least two questions:

### Question 1

> **Can God communicate X truthfully?**

If God genuinely communicates X, then yes, because God cannot lie.

### Question 2

> **Did God actually communicate X to this person?**

That is an authentication question.

The first question concerns God's nature.

The second concerns evidence.

The two must not be conflated.

---

# 11. God's Inability to Lie Does Not Authenticate Human Claims

This is where many arguments become circular.

Consider:

> “God cannot lie.”

Therefore:

> “This document is true.”

That inference is invalid unless the missing premise has been established:

> **“This document genuinely comes from God.”**

The proper structure is:

> **God cannot lie.**

+

> **This communication genuinely comes from God.**

Therefore:

> **This genuine divine communication is truthful.**

The second premise still requires authentication.

This is precisely why the book does not jump from Chapter 12 directly to:

> “Therefore the Bible is infallible.”

That conclusion belongs later, after the investigation of:

- what the Bible is;
- what kind of record it is;
- how revelation was given;
- witnesses;
- Christ;
- apostles;
- inspiration;
- canon;
- historical testimony;
- and cumulative authentication.

The architecture is deliberately preventing circular reasoning.

---

# 12. God's Truthfulness and the Reliability of His Word

The preceding chapters have prepared a second important conclusion.

If God's genuine communication is truthful, then God's Word cannot be treated as though it were merely one fallible human opinion among others.

The issue is not that human beings automatically understand everything God communicates.

That is a different question.

There is a crucial distinction between:

> **truthfulness of the source**

and:

> **accuracy of the receiver's interpretation.**

God may communicate truthfully while a human being misunderstands what God has communicated.

Therefore:

> **Divine truthfulness does not imply human interpretive infallibility.**

This distinction will become essential later when the book addresses Scripture and interpretation.

The authority of the text must not be confused with the authority of every interpretation of the text.

---

# 13. God's Truthfulness Does Not Eliminate the Need for Human Reason

The same distinction applies to reasoning.

If God cannot lie, it does not follow that every human conclusion about God's Word is automatically true.

A person can possess an infallible text and reason fallibly about it.

They can:

- quote the wrong passage;
- misunderstand context;
- confuse two meanings of a word;
- draw an invalid inference;
- ignore a qualification;
- mistake metaphor for literal description;
- or force a conclusion the text does not establish.

Therefore the reader still needs:

> **knowledge, evidence, reasoning, judgment, skill, and disciplined interpretation.**

This is not a concession to human authority over Scripture.

It is recognition of human fallibility.

The text can be authoritative while the reader remains responsible for understanding it correctly.

---

# 14. God's Truthfulness and God's Faithfulness Are Not Identical

Chapter 11 distinguished these attributes, and the distinction remains important here.

### Truthfulness

Concerns the incompatibility of falsehood with God's nature.

### Faithfulness

Concerns God's dependable adherence to His Word, covenant, and promises.

A truthful statement and a faithful promise are related but not identical.

For example, someone might tell the truth about what exists while failing to keep a promise.

The biblical conception of God does not leave that gap.

God is:

> **true**

and:

> **faithful.**

Therefore His communication is not merely accurate in content; His commitments are dependable in execution.

This becomes important when the biblical record later presents fulfilled prophecy, historical action, covenant fulfillment, and the correspondence between God's Word and events.

---

# 15. God's Truthfulness and Immutability Are Also Related

Immutability adds another layer.

Suppose a being were truthful today but could fundamentally become false tomorrow.

Its previous truthfulness would not provide permanent epistemic security.

But the biblical conception of God does not permit that instability.

Hebrews 6:17 speaks of:

> **“the immutability of his counsel.”**

James 1:17 speaks of:

> **“no variableness, neither shadow of turning.”**

Therefore:

> **God's inability to lie is not an isolated momentary characteristic.**

It belongs to the stable character of God.

The God who is true does not later become false.

The God who is faithful does not later become faithless.

The God whose counsel is immutable does not reverse Himself through a corruption of character.

This is why truthfulness, faithfulness, and immutability form a coherent foundation for trustworthy revelation.

---

# 16. 2 Timothy 2:13 — “He Cannot Deny Himself”

Paul writes:

> **“if we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.”**

This statement adds another dimension.

The issue is not simply:

> “God has a rule against lying.”

The statement:

> **“he cannot deny himself”**

points again toward the relationship between God's actions and His identity.

God remains faithful because He cannot become contrary to Himself.

This gives us a useful conceptual formulation:

> **God cannot truthfully become false to His own nature.**

His truthfulness is not an external costume.

It belongs to Him.

Therefore falsehood is not merely an unacceptable behavior that He happens to avoid.

It is contrary to His identity.

---

# 17. 1 John 1:5 — No Darkness in Him

John gives another important description:

> **“God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.”**

The statement is not merely poetic decoration.

It contributes to the biblical picture of God's moral and epistemic purity.

If:

> **God is light**

and:

> **“in him is no darkness at all,”**
